subject: English
title: Anaya's Special Letters
hook: Write kind letters to friends and family the right way

characters.name: Grandpa
characters.role: lives far away in another city

slides.title: Letter Writing
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother shows her a blue envelope. Inside is a handwritten letter from Grandpa in Delhi, asking about her school life. Anaya wants to write back.
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters are friendly messages we write by hand to someone we care about.

image.alt: Letter Writing — Letter Writing

slides.title: Why We Write Letters
slides.storyContext: Anaya learned that Grandpa's eyes get tired on his computer. A paper letter makes him very happy because he can hold it, read it slowly, and keep it forever. Her mother says: 'Your words on paper are like a warm hug.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters show people we care, and they treasure them.

image.alt: Why We Write Letters — Letter Writing

slides.title: Letters Are Special Gifts
slides.storyContext: Anaya sits with her mother and listens: 'Letters are different from emails or messages. They take time. They feel real. People keep them in boxes and read them again and again, remembering your love. When you write a letter, you give someone the best gift—your thought and your heart.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A letter is a present that keeps giving, every time the reader opens it.

slides.title: Parts of a Friendly Letter
slides.storyContext: Anaya sits at the kitchen table with pencil and paper. Her mother shows her the five parts of a letter using her fingers.

points.label: Date
points.text: Write the day at the top (e.g., 15 June 2026)

points.label: Greeting
points.text: Start with 'Dear Grandpa,' or 'Hello Ria,'

points.label: Body
points.text: Tell your news and feelings (2-3 sentences)

points.label: Closing
points.text: End with 'Your loving granddaughter,' or 'With love,'

points.label: Signature
points.text: Sign your name below the closing

slides.inSimpleWords: Every letter has five parts—like a body has head, arms, and legs.

image.alt: Parts of a Friendly Letter — Letter Writing

slides.title: Anaya's First Try
slides.storyContext: Anaya picks up her pencil. 'I'm nervous,' she whispers. Her mother smiles: 'You know what to do. You have five boxes to fill. Box 1: the date. Box 2: say hello. Box 3: tell your story. Box 4: say goodbye. Box 5: sign your name. Go!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every letter is a simple puzzle—five boxes, and your heart fills them.

slides.title: Writing the Date and Greeting
slides.storyContext: Anaya writes on her paper: '20 June 2026' at the top. Then she skips a line and writes: 'Dear Grandpa,'

points.text: Write today's date on the first line
Use a comma after the person's name in the greeting
Keep it warm but respectful (Dear, Hello, Hi work fine)

slides.inSimpleWords: The date and greeting welcome the reader into your letter.

image.alt: Writing the Date and Greeting — Letter Writing

slides.title: Date and Greeting in Action
slides.storyContext: Anaya's pencil moves: '20 June 2026' on the first line, blank line, then 'Dear Grandpa,' She says it aloud: 'It sounds nice!'

example.problem: Write the date and greeting for a letter to your mother.
example.solution:
28 June 2026

Dear Mama,

slides.inSimpleWords: The date tells when you wrote it. The greeting is your 'hello.'

slides.title: The Body: Your Message
slides.storyContext: Anaya writes: 'I hope you are well. I got 95 in my maths test today! I also played a new game at school called Tag. My friend Ria and I won our team. I miss you very much.'

points.text: Share real news from your life (school, friends, hobbies)
Use simple, clear sentences (2-4 sentences is perfect)
Tell how you feel (happy, proud, sad, excited)
Ask about the other person (How are you? What are you doing?)

slides.inSimpleWords: The body is your heart—share what matters to you.

image.alt: The Body: Your Message — Letter Writing

slides.title: What Should I Say?
slides.storyContext: Anaya bites her pencil. 'What do I write about, Mama?' Her mother laughs: 'Think of what made you happy today. Did you learn something? Did you play with a friend? Did you try something new? Tell Grandpa these things. Tell him three good things. Then ask him one question. That's enough!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Your body tells a story—your day, your feelings, your questions.

slides.title: Body Examples for Different People
slides.storyContext: Anaya looks at what other kids wrote in their bodies:

example.problem: What are two good body paragraphs?
example.solution:
To Grandpa: 'I won the spelling bee! My team beat Class 4. I wish you were here to see it. How is your garden growing?'

To friend Ria: 'We made art today with paints and paper. I made a butterfly. It was so fun! Can you come play after school tomorrow?'

slides.inSimpleWords: Different people, different messages—but always true and warm.

slides.title: The Closing and Signature
slides.storyContext: Anaya finishes writing: 'With lots of love, Anaya' at the bottom. She reads it aloud, and it sounds just right.

points.text: Choose a warm closing: 'With love,', 'Your loving...', 'All my love,'
Skip a line and write your name
Your signature shows the letter came from your heart

slides.inSimpleWords: The closing is a hug—it shows you care.

image.alt: The Closing and Signature — Letter Writing

slides.title: Signing with Your Whole Heart
slides.storyContext: Anaya holds her pencil high. 'My name is Anaya,' she says proudly, writing each letter slowly. Her mother says: 'When you sign, you're saying to Grandpa: this letter is really from me, really from my heart, really from my hands. Your name is your promise.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Your signature is your stamp—it means 'This is really from me.'

slides.title: Closings That Work Best

points.label: For Grandparents
points.text: 'With lots of love,' or 'Your loving granddaughter,'

points.label: For Friends
points.text: 'Your best friend,' or 'With giggles,'

points.label: For Teachers
points.text: 'Respectfully,' or 'Your student,'

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose a closing that fits the person and how you feel.

slides.title: A Real Letter from Anaya
slides.storyContext: Here is the complete letter Anaya wrote to Grandpa.

example.problem: Write a friendly letter following all five parts.
example.solution:
20 June 2026

Dear Grandpa,

I hope you are well. I got 95 in my maths test today! I played cricket at school and scored 20 runs. I miss you so much and want you to visit soon. How are you? Are you eating well?

With lots of love,
Anaya

slides.inSimpleWords: A good letter is honest, warm, and easy to read.

image.alt: A Real Letter from Anaya — Letter Writing

slides.title: The Envelope and the Stamp
slides.storyContext: Anaya folds her letter carefully. Her mother shows her how to address an envelope: 'Top left is your name. Bottom right is Grandpa's name and city. The stamp goes top right. It's like the letter's travel ticket!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The envelope carries your words safely to someone far away.

slides.title: Write Your Own Letter
slides.storyContext: Ria's birthday is coming. Anaya decides to write her a birthday letter. 'I want to tell her how special she is to me,' Anaya thinks.

example.problem: Write a short friendly letter to a friend, including all five parts. Share a happy memory or tell them why they are special.
example.solution:
15 July 2026

Dear Ria,

Happy birthday to my best friend! I remember when we first met in Class 1 and we shared our lunch. Now we play together every day. You make me laugh and you are kind to everyone. I am so lucky to have you as a friend. Let's have fun at your birthday party!

With love,
Anaya

slides.inSimpleWords: When you write a letter, imagine sitting with the person and talking to them.

image.alt: Write Your Own Letter — Letter Writing

slides.title: Grandpa Writes Back
slides.storyContext: One week later, Anaya comes home to find a blue envelope on the table. Her mother gives it to her with a smile. Inside, Grandpa has written: 'Dear Anaya, Your letter made me the happiest grandpa in Delhi. I read it three times. I am proud of your maths. Come visit soon. Love, Grandpa'
slides.inSimpleWords: The best part of writing letters is the reply that comes back—proof that someone cares.

slides.title: Why Letters Matter More Than Messages

points.label: Take Time
points.text: They show you took the trouble to write by hand

points.label: Last Forever
points.text: People keep them in boxes and reread them years later

points.label: Feel Real
points.text: You can see your handwriting, smell the paper, hold it close

points.label: Show Love
points.text: Every word says 'You are worth my time and thought'

slides.inSimpleWords: Messages fade. Letters stay. Letters say 'I love you' louder than any text.

slides.title: Fix This Letter (Find the Mistakes)
slides.storyContext: Anaya's cousin Rohan wrote a letter but made mistakes. Can you spot them?

example.problem:
Find the five errors in this letter:

20 june 2026
Dear Ria
I had fun with you yesterday. We played. It was nice.
With love
Rohan
example.solution:
1. Month should be capitalized: June (not june)
2. Greeting needs a comma: Dear Ria, (not Dear Ria)
3. Body is too short—add details!
4. Closing needs a comma: With love, (not With love)
5. Add a line break before signature

slides.inSimpleWords: Good letters have details, proper punctuation, and warmth.

slides.title: Letters Across India
slides.storyContext: Anaya learns that her grandmother in Mumbai, her aunt in Bangalore, and her cousin in Hyderabad all treasure the letters they get. 'Letters connect us,' her mother says. 'When someone lives far away, a letter is like a bridge of words bringing them close again.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters travel across deserts and mountains to touch someone's heart.

slides.title: Anaya Becomes a Letter Writer
slides.storyContext: By the end of summer, Anaya has written letters to Grandpa, Ria, her teacher, and her aunt. People smile when they see her name on an envelope. 'You have a gift,' her mother says, 'for making people feel loved.' Anaya beams with pride.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you write letters, you become a giver of happiness.

slides.title: Challenge: Write to Someone New
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. Think of someone you love or admire—maybe a cousin, uncle, teacher, or friend. Write them a letter using all five parts. Make it warm and honest.

example.problem: Choose a person and write a complete five-part letter to them.
example.solution: Remember: Date, Greeting, Body (3-4 sentences with real news), Closing, and Signature. Take your time. Your words matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every letter you write is an act of love—don't be shy.

slides.title: Letters Through History
slides.storyContext: Anaya's grandmother shows her a stack of old letters tied with ribbon. These are from her mother, Anaya's great-grandmother. She lived in a village without phones or internet. These letters kept us connected across hundreds of miles. Anaya holds them carefully, feeling the weight of love across generations.
slides.inSimpleWords: Letters are time capsules of love—they last forever.

slides.title: Special Types of Letters

points.label: Thank-You Letters
points.text: Express gratitude for a gift, help, or kind gesture

points.label: Apology Letters
points.text: Say sorry, explain why, and promise to do better

points.label: Love Letters
points.text: Tell someone how much they mean to you

points.label: Birthday Letters
points.text: Celebrate someone's special day in a personal way

slides.inSimpleWords: Each type of letter has its own warmth and purpose.

slides.title: Mix and Match Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya gets creative. She decides to write three different types of letters in one day.

example.problem: Write: (1) a thank-you letter to a teacher, (2) an apology letter to a friend, (3) a birthday letter to a sibling.
example.solution: Each should follow the five parts but with different tones. Thank-you: warm and grateful. Apology: honest and sincere. Birthday: joyful and celebratory.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice different letter types—become a master letter writer.

slides.title: Anaya's Letter Legacy
slides.storyContext: Years later, Anaya's friends and family will treasure her letters. Her grandpa will reread her letters during lonely nights. Her best friend will keep them in a box. Her mother will show them to Anaya's children someday and say: This is how your mother loved us.
slides.inSimpleWords: Your letters today become someone's treasure tomorrow.

slides.title: Five Steps to Write a Letter

points.text: Write the date at the top
Use a greeting like 'Dear...' with a comma
Share real news and feelings in the body (2-4 sentences)
Close with a warm ending like 'With love,'
Sign your name—show it came from your heart

slides.inSimpleWords: Letters are love in an envelope—take time, be honest, and share your heart.

image.alt: Five Steps to Write a Letter — Letter Writing

subject: English
title: Vikram's Tale of the Clever Fox
hook: Enjoy stories full of adventure, animals, and life lessons

characters.name: Teacher Meera
characters.role: brings stories to life in class

slides.title: Story Reading
slides.storyContext: Vikram sits in the village library after school. Teacher Meera comes to him with a brown book of stories. 'Today, I have a story of a very clever fox,' she says, opening to the first page.
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories are journeys—take them with all your heart and imagination.

image.alt: Story Reading — Story Reading

slides.title: The Story Begins
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera reads: 'Once, a hungry fox came to a village. He saw a farmer's henhouse. But the gate had a lock. How would he get inside?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every story starts with 'once upon a time' and a problem to solve.

image.alt: The Story Begins — Story Reading

slides.title: The Fox's Journey (Middle of the Tale)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera continues: 'The fox tried to dig under the fence. He worked all night. By dawn, he had a tunnel. He squeezed through, closer and closer to the hens. But then—the farmer's dog barked! The fox's heart raced.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories rise and fall—they have exciting middles where things get tricky.

slides.title: Story Elements: Characters
slides.storyContext: Vikram learns that stories have heroes, villains, and helpers. The fox is clever and hungry. The farmer is kind but needs to protect his hens. The hens are innocent and scared.

points.text: Characters are the people and animals in the story
Main character (hero): the fox trying to solve a problem
Supporting characters: the farmer, the hens
Each character has feelings and reasons for what they do

slides.inSimpleWords: Characters are like people in real life—each one is different and special.

image.alt: Story Elements: Characters — Story Reading

slides.title: Know Your Characters
slides.storyContext: Vikram asks: 'But why does the fox want the hens?' Teacher Meera explains: 'He's hungry. Foxes hunt to survive. The farmer protects his hens because that's his job. Nobody is purely evil—they just have different needs.'

example.problem: Why does each character act the way they do?
example.solution:
Fox: He's hungry and wants to eat.
Farmer: He works hard and owns the hens—he must protect them.
Hens: They are scared because foxes hunt them.
Each character has a reason.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good stories show why people act the way they do.

slides.title: Story Elements: Plot (What Happens)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera shows Vikram the story's arc: Problem (fox hungry, henhouse locked) → Attempt (fox digs under the fence) → Climax (he almost gets in!) → Twist (farmer catches him!) → Ending (fox runs away and learns a lesson).

points.text: Problem: What is the challenge or trouble?
Rising Action: What does the character try? Does it work?
Climax: The most exciting or important moment
Ending: How is the problem solved? What lesson was learned?

slides.inSimpleWords: A plot is like climbing a hill—up, up, peak, then down to peace.

image.alt: Story Elements: Plot (What Happens) — Story Reading

slides.title: The Climax (Most Exciting Part)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera's voice gets loud and fast: 'The fox pushed through the tunnel. The hens screamed. The farmer ran out with a stick. The dog barked and barked. The fox turned and RAN! The farmer chased him all the way to the forest edge!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The climax is where everything shakes—where you hold your breath.

slides.title: Story Elements: Setting (Where and When)
slides.storyContext: The fox's story happens in a village at dawn. It takes place on the outskirts of a farm, near a henhouse, under a big mango tree. The time of year is summer when foxes are hungriest.

points.text: Setting tells WHERE the story happens (village, forest, house, city)
Setting tells WHEN it happens (morning, summer, long ago, today)
The setting affects what happens (a sleepy village is different from a busy market)

slides.inSimpleWords: Setting is the stage where the story dances—it shapes everything.

image.alt: Story Elements: Setting (Where and When) — Story Reading

slides.title: The Ending (What We Learn)
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera's voice becomes calm and thoughtful: 'The fox sat in the forest, panting. He had tried so hard but failed. That night, he found a dead rabbit left by a hunter. He ate it and thought: sometimes trying to steal is harder and more dangerous than finding honest food. The fox learned that day.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Endings teach us—they show what happens when someone learns.

slides.title: The Lesson (Moral) of the Story
slides.storyContext: Vikram finishes reading and asks: 'What does this story teach us?' Teacher Meera smiles: 'The fox was clever, but being cunning doesn't always win. The farmer's honesty and kindness are stronger. Also, respecting others' things keeps you safe.'

points.text: Every good story has a lesson or moral (a teaching about life)
The lesson might be about kindness, honesty, hard work, or courage
The ending shows the lesson by what happens to the characters

slides.inSimpleWords: Every story whispers: 'This is how to live a good life.'

image.alt: The Lesson (Moral) of the Story — Story Reading

slides.title: A Complete Story for You
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera reads Vikram a short tale: 'There was a kind boy named Arjun. He found a hungry kitten on the street. He gave it milk and rice every day. Soon, the kitten became strong and healthy. It played with Arjun and they became best friends. The whole village loved them both.'

example.problem: Find: (1) Main character? (2) Setting? (3) Problem? (4) How was it solved? (5) What is the lesson?
example.solution: (1) Arjun and the kitten. (2) The street and Arjun's home. (3) Hungry kitten, lonely Arjun. (4) Arjun fed the kitten and cared for it. (5) Kindness brings friendship and happiness.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good stories show how kind hearts change the world.

image.alt: A Complete Story for You — Story Reading

slides.title: Stories Connect Us
slides.storyContext: After the story, Vikram asks Teacher Meera: 'Are there really clever foxes like that?' She smiles: 'Foxes do exist, and they are clever. But this story is also made up—it's a fable, a tale with a lesson. Thousands of children in India have read this same story. We all feel the same feelings when we read it.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories are bridges—they connect our hearts across time and place.

slides.title: Story Spot (Find the Elements)
slides.storyContext: Vikram reads a new short story: 'Priya lived in a small town by the river. One day, a storm came. The river flooded. Priya's neighbors were scared. She led everyone to the high ground of the old temple. All were safe. Priya became the village hero.'

example.problem: Identify: (1) Who is the hero? (2) What is the problem? (3) Where does it happen? (4) When does it happen? (5) What is the lesson?
example.solution: (1) Priya. (2) A flood from a storm. (3) A river town, at the temple. (4) During a storm/sudden crisis. (5) Courage and quick thinking save lives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Great readers spot every part of a story—characters, plot, setting, and lesson.

image.alt: Story Spot (Find the Elements) — Story Reading

slides.title: Different Types of Stories

points.label: Fables
points.text: Short stories with animals that teach a moral (like the fox story)

points.label: Folktales
points.text: Old stories passed down through families and cultures

points.label: Adventures
points.text: Exciting stories with travel, danger, and heroism

points.label: Fairytales
points.text: Magical stories with princes, princesses, and magic

slides.inSimpleWords: Stories come in many flavors—each kind teaches or delights us differently.

slides.title: Vikram Becomes a Story Reader
slides.storyContext: Week after week, Vikram and Teacher Meera read together. He finds himself sitting under the mango tree with a book, lost in stories. He reads about princesses in palaces, animals in forests, and children solving mysteries. Each story teaches him something new about courage, kindness, and the world.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you start reading stories, you become a traveler to a thousand worlds.

slides.title: Retell a Story
slides.storyContext: Think of a story you know—from your family, your culture, or a book. Retell it to a friend using the story elements: Who are the characters? What is the problem? Where and when does it happen? What is the lesson?

example.problem: Retell a story using all four elements.
example.solution: Characters: (names/roles), Setting: (where and when), Problem: (the main trouble), Lesson: (what we learn)

slides.inSimpleWords: Every story you know is a gift—share it with others.

slides.title: Reading Creates Empathy
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera asks Vikram: 'When you read about the fox, you felt his hunger, his cunning, his disappointment. When you read about Priya, you felt her courage. This is empathy—you feel what the character feels. That makes you kinder in real life.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories teach us to feel what others feel.

slides.title: How to Read Deeper

points.label: Ask Why
points.text: Why does the character act this way? What do they want?

points.label: Notice Details
points.text: What does the story tell us about the setting, time, or mood?

points.label: Predict Ahead
points.text: What do you think will happen next? Why?

points.label: Reflect After
points.text: What did you learn? How does it change you?

slides.inSimpleWords: Deep reading means asking questions and thinking hard.

slides.title: Reading Practice: A Mystery Story
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera reads: 'A girl found a locked box in her attic. Inside was a letter from her great-grandmother. It said: I hid the truth about our family. Now you're old enough to know. The girl's hands shook.'

example.problem: Stop here and predict: What is the truth? What will the girl do next? What lesson might this story teach?
example.solution: Many answers are possible: She might discover a hidden relative, a secret talent, a forgotten recipe. The lesson might be about family, truth, or courage. That's what makes stories beautiful—we all imagine differently.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every reader imagines the story uniquely—that's the magic.

slides.title: Create Your Own Character
slides.storyContext: Now Vikram tries to create his own story character. He thinks: Who will my hero be? What do they want? What problem will they face?

example.problem: Invent a character. Write: (1) Their name and age, (2) What they want more than anything, (3) One strength, (4) One weakness, (5) A problem they face.
example.solution: Example: Asha, age 9, wants to be a cricket player. Strength: fast runner. Weakness: afraid to fail. Problem: her family says girls shouldn't play sports.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every good story starts with a person we care about.

slides.title: Stories Show Different Worlds
slides.storyContext: Vikram reads stories from different countries—folktales from Japan, Africa, South America. He learns that stories are universal. Every culture tells tales of courage, love, and wisdom.
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories connect us to people everywhere.

slides.title: Story Mapping
slides.storyContext: Teacher Meera teaches Vikram to map a story visually—drawing the beginning, middle, and end.

example.problem: Draw or write a story map: Left side (beginning: setting and characters), Middle (rising action and climax), Right side (resolution and lesson).
example.solution: The fox story: Beginning (fox hungry, henhouse locked), Middle (fox digs tunnel, almost gets in), Climax (farmer catches him), End (fox runs away, learns a lesson).

slides.inSimpleWords: Visual maps help you see the story's shape.

slides.title: Vikram's Reading Journey
slides.storyContext: By the end of summer, Vikram has read 20 stories. He can spot characters, plot twists, and lessons instantly. But more importantly, he loves stories. He reads before bed, at lunch, in the park. Stories are now part of his life.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you love reading, stories become your best friends.

slides.title: Write Your Own Short Story
slides.storyContext: Vikram is ready to write his own story. He has characters in mind, a problem, and an idea for an ending.

example.problem: Write a short story (5-10 sentences) with: a hero, a clear problem, at least one attempt to solve it, a climax, and a lesson.
example.solution: Story: A boy named Dev found a hurt bird. He made a nest, fed it, stayed with it all week. When it flew away, Dev felt sad but proud. He learned: sometimes love means letting go.

slides.inSimpleWords: You have all the tools—now tell your story.

slides.title: Stories Connect Hearts
slides.storyContext: Vikram realizes that when he reads a story, he's not alone. Thousands of children have read the same fox tale. They all laughed at the same moments, felt scared during the same climax, and learned the same lesson. Stories are like bridges connecting hearts across time.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you read a story, you join millions of readers across the world.

slides.title: Story Detective Challenge
slides.storyContext: Vikram becomes a Story Detective. He reads a new story and must solve five mysteries before moving on.

example.problem:
For any story you read, answer:
1. Who is the main character?
2. What do they want or need?
3. What stops them from getting it?
4. How do they overcome it?
5. What do they learn?
example.solution: These five questions unlock the heart of every story. Master them, and you can understand any tale.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every story has secrets. Learn to find them.

slides.title: Real Stories vs. Made-Up Stories

points.label: Real Stories (Nonfiction)
points.text: True events that really happened—biographies, history, news

points.label: Made-Up Stories (Fiction)
points.text: Invented tales with imaginary characters and events

points.label: Mix
points.text: Some stories blend both—real events with added details or emotions

slides.inSimpleWords: Both real and imaginary stories teach us—in different ways.

slides.title: Vikram's Story Collection
slides.storyContext: By year's end, Vikram has read 30 stories. He keeps them all in his mind like a library. He can revisit them anytime. He tells them to his little sister at bedtime. He shares them with friends. Stories have become his superpower.
slides.inSimpleWords: Stories you read stay with you forever—they shape who you become.

slides.title: How to Enjoy Stories

points.text: Learn the characters—understand their feelings and choices
Follow the plot—beginning, middle, end, and how it's solved
Notice the setting—where and when the story happens
Find the lesson—what the story teaches about life
Use imagination—picture the story like a movie in your mind

slides.inSimpleWords: Stories are mirrors of life—read them slowly and let them speak to your heart.

image.alt: How to Enjoy Stories — Story Reading

subject: English
title: Maya's Rainbow of Words
hook: Feel the magic of poems that sing and dance

slides.title: Poetry
slides.storyContext: Rain falls on the roof of Maya's school. Poet Uncle visits Class 3 and opens a slim book of poems. 'Today, we feel with words!' he says, and reads: 'Pitter-patter, pitter-pat, raindrops dance on the mat.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is language playing music—words that sing, rhyme, and paint pictures.

image.alt: Poetry — Poetry

slides.title: Why Poets Write
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle tells Maya: 'I write poems to catch feelings in words. When I see a butterfly, I feel free. When I hear a child laugh, I feel joy. Poems say big feelings in small, beautiful ways. A poem is a gift of the heart.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poems let us say how we feel when words aren't enough.

image.alt: Why Poets Write — Poetry

slides.title: Poetry Lives Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle claps his hands: 'Poetry isn't just in books. It's in songs you hear on the radio. It's in nursery rhymes. It's in prayers. It's in a mother's lullaby. Listen! You'll find poetry hiding all around you.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry isn't rare—it's everywhere, singing if you listen closely.

slides.title: Rhyme: Words That Sound Alike
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle claps and reads: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, How I wonder what you are!' Maya claps too—'star' and 'are' sound the same!'

points.text: Rhyme is when two words sound alike at the end (cat, bat; moon, soon)
Rhyming words make poems fun to read and easy to remember
Rhyming patterns can be AABB (first two lines rhyme, next two rhyme) or ABAB

example.problem: Find the rhyming words: 'The cat sat on a mat, She wore a funny hat.'
example.solution: sat/mat rhyme (A), hat rhymes with them too. This is AAA rhyme.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhyme is poetry's music—when words dance to the same beat.

image.alt: Rhyme: Words That Sound Alike — Poetry

slides.title: Rhyme Makes Us Remember
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle laughs: 'Do you know your ABCs? A-B-C-D-E-F-G... You remember it because it rhymes! When a poem rhymes, it sticks in your brain like glue. You can recite it months later!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rhyming poems are sticky—your brain loves them and remembers.

slides.title: Rhythm: The Heartbeat of Words
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle drums on the table: 'Boom-boom-BOOM, boom-boom-BOOM. Listen to the pattern.' Maya walks to the beat, then reads a poem the same way. The words have rhythm!

points.text: Rhythm is the beat you hear when you read a poem aloud
Some syllables are strong (BOOM), some soft (boom)
Rhythm makes poems fun to say and hear

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhythm is the drum inside the poem—tap along and feel it.

image.alt: Rhythm: The Heartbeat of Words — Poetry

slides.title: Feel the Rhythm
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads aloud and taps: 'The rain goes pit-ter-PAT-ter (tap tap TAP tap), On leaves of green and YEL-low.' Maya stamps her foot: she can feel the beat!

example.problem: Mark the strong beat (stress) in this line: 'The SNOW fell SOFT and WHITE and COLD'
example.solution: The SNOW fell SOFT and WHITE and COLD — every other syllable is stressed

slides.inSimpleWords: When you read a poem aloud, your body feels the rhythm.

slides.title: Simile: Comparing Two Things
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads: 'Her smile is bright like the sun.' Maya thinks: 'Oh! A smile is not really the sun, but it shines like the sun does. That's beautiful!'

points.text: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'
It helps us see something in a new, beautiful way
Examples: as strong as a tiger, bright like a star, soft as cotton

example.problem: Complete the simile: 'The river flows like _____' or 'Her voice is sweet as _____'
example.solution: The river flows like a snake. Her voice is sweet as honey.

slides.inSimpleWords: Similes are word pictures—they say 'this is like that' to show beauty.

image.alt: Simile: Comparing Two Things — Poetry

slides.title: Similes in Everyday Life
slides.storyContext: Maya notices: 'Poet Uncle, my grandmother says I'm 'busy as a bee.' Is that a simile?' Poet Uncle nods proudly: 'Yes! You found one! People use similes all the time. Your mother might say you're 'good as gold' or 'stubborn as a mule.' Those are all similes hiding in regular talk!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Similes are everywhere—even in how people talk every day.

slides.title: Metaphor: One Thing IS Another
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads: 'Life is a journey.' Maya asks: 'But life isn't really a journey!' He smiles: 'In poetry, we can say life IS a journey because we grow and learn, just like travelers move ahead.'

points.text: A metaphor says one thing IS another (not 'like' another)
It makes us think deeply about the hidden meaning
Examples: 'Time is gold', 'Her heart is stone', 'Hope is a bird'

slides.inSimpleWords: Metaphors are magic—they make one thing become another in our minds.

image.alt: Metaphor: One Thing IS Another — Poetry

slides.title: Metaphor Magic
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle leans in: 'If I say 'Her heart is a stone,' I don't mean her heart is literally a rock. I mean she acts cold, hard to move, unfeeling. Metaphors take invisible feelings and give them shape. They make the invisible visible.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Metaphors transform feelings into things we can almost touch.

slides.title: A Poem About Rain
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle reads a complete poem for Maya:

example.problem: Read and find: (1) Rhyming words, (2) A simile, (3) The feeling of the poem.
example.solution:
Poem: 'Pitter-patter, pat-pat-pat, rain falls like a dancing cat. Splish and splash on the ground, nature's music is the sound. Wet and cold and fresh and free, rain brings joy to you and me.'

(1) pat/cat, ground/sound, free/me rhyme.
(2) Simile: 'rain falls like a dancing cat'
(3) Joy, playfulness, and love of nature.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry shows us the beauty hiding in everyday things.

image.alt: A Poem About Rain — Poetry

slides.title: Write Your Own Poem
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle gives Maya a challenge: 'Write a short poem about something you love. It can be about your pet, your home, a friend, or nature. Use rhyming words and a simile if you can!'

example.problem: Write a 4-line poem about your favorite thing. Include at least one rhyme and one simile.
example.solution: My puppy is sweet like honey on bread, She plays with me from dawn till bed. Her eyes shine bright like stars so clear, I love my puppy, she's so dear!

slides.inSimpleWords: Poets are word artists—paint feelings, rhymes, and pictures on paper.

image.alt: Write Your Own Poem — Poetry

slides.title: Maya Finds Her Poet's Voice
slides.storyContext: By the end of class, Maya has written three poems—one about her mother's hands, one about the monsoon, one about her puppy. Poet Uncle reads them aloud with feeling. 'These are real poems,' he says. 'You have something to say, and you're saying it in the most beautiful way.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When you write a poem, you're speaking the language of the heart.

slides.title: Identify the Poetry Device
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle shows Maya lines from different poems. Can she spot the rhyme, simile, metaphor, or rhythm?

example.problem:
What poetry device is in each line?
1. 'The sun danced across the sky'
2. 'Soft as silk and smooth as cream'
3. 'Rain falls pit-ter-PAT-ter, pit-ter-PAT-ter'
example.solution:
1. Metaphor (sun danced—sun doesn't really dance)
2. Simile (soft as, smooth as)
3. Rhythm (the beat is clear)

slides.inSimpleWords: Great poets know all the tricks—rhyme, rhythm, simile, metaphor.

slides.title: Poetry Lives in Your Heart
slides.storyContext: At the end of class, Poet Uncle sits with Maya and says: 'You don't need permission to write a poem. You just need a pencil and a feeling. A worry. A memory. A dream. A joy. Write about it in words that sing, and you're a poet.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Everyone is a poet—you just need to feel something and let words flow.

slides.title: More Poetry Devices: Alliteration and Sound

points.label: Alliteration
points.text: Repeating the same sound at the start of words: pretty pink petals

points.label: Onomatopoeia
points.text: Words that sound like their meaning: buzz, hiss, boom, splash

points.label: Repetition
points.text: Saying the same words over and over for effect

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry has many tricks—learn them all.

slides.title: Find the Devices
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle shares examples of each device:

example.problem:
Spot the device in each line:
1. The bee buzzed busily by the big blue building
2. Crash! Bang! Boom! The thunder roared.
3. Never, never give up! Never, never stop dreaming!
example.solution:
1. Alliteration (B sound repeats)
2. Onomatopoeia (crash, bang, boom sound like the noise)
3. Repetition (never, never...repeats)

slides.inSimpleWords: Great poems use every trick in the book.

slides.title: Poets Are Dreamers
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle tells Maya: 'Poets see the world differently. They notice a spider web covered in dewdrops and see diamonds. They hear a child cry and feel the weight of the world. They love too much, dream too big, feel too deeply. That's why we read their poems—to feel alive.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Poets are sensitive souls who share their hearts through words.

slides.title: Create a Poetry Slam Entry
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle invites students to write and perform poems for a class poetry slam—a celebration of student poets.

example.problem: Write a poem (any length) and be ready to read it aloud with feeling.
example.solution: Include: rhyme (at least 2 lines), rhythm (a beat you can tap), and one comparison (simile or metaphor). Most important: say something TRUE.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is for sharing—read it aloud and let others feel your words.

slides.title: Poems From India
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle shares poems by Rabindranath Tagore, Sarojini Naidu, and other Indian poets. These poets wrote about nature, love, freedom, and India itself. Their words shaped a nation. Your words matter too.
slides.inSimpleWords: India has a rich poetry tradition—you are part of it.

slides.title: Poetry Journal
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle gives Maya a journal. Write one small poem every day for a week. About anything. Don't worry about perfect rhymes or rhythm. Just feel and write.

example.problem: Keep a poetry journal for 7 days. Topics: joy, sadness, nature, friendship, hope, fear, gratitude.
example.solution: Day 1 (joy): Ice cream melts, sweet and cold, a moment of pure happiness. Day 2 (sadness): Empty chair at the table, silence where laughter used to be.

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry journals capture your feelings before they fade.

slides.title: Maya Becomes a Poet
slides.storyContext: By the end of the season, Maya has written 30 poems. Some are short, some long. Some rhyme, some don't. All of them are hers. She reads them to her parents, her friends, and her dog. They all listen, and they all feel something.
slides.inSimpleWords: You don't have to be famous to be a poet—you just have to feel.

slides.title: Write a Poem About Your Life
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. Write a poem about something important to you—a place, a person, a dream, or a feeling.

example.problem: Write a 4-8 line poem. Include: rhyme (at least 2 lines), one comparison (simile or metaphor), and rhythm (a beat).
example.solution: Example: My home is a fort of love (metaphor), Where laughter dances like fireflies (simile). My mother's arms wrap warm and soft, My father's jokes make my belly hurt with giggles (rhythm). This is my safe place (metaphor), This is where I belong.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your life deserves a poem. Write it.

slides.title: Poetry is Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Poet Uncle's final lesson: Poetry isn't just in books. It's in your mother's prayers. It's in your grandmother's lullabies. It's in songs, prayers, and even in how people speak when they're heartbroken. Poetry is the language of the soul. You're a poet already—you just didn't know it.
slides.inSimpleWords: You are already a poet. Now own it.

slides.title: Poetry Magic

points.text: Rhyme makes poetry sound beautiful (words with the same ending sound)
Rhythm is the beat you feel when you read aloud
Similes compare using 'like' or 'as' (bright like a star)
Metaphors make one thing become another (life is a journey)
Poetry shows big feelings in small, beautiful words

slides.inSimpleWords: Poetry is the art of feeling with words—read it slowly, say it aloud, and let it touch your heart.
